name: Tholung Monastery
tagline: Upper Dzongu's relic monastery, opened every three years
meta_description: Tholung Monastery, Upper Dzongu: 18th-century Nyingma gompa whose sealed relics are shown at the Kamsel every three years. Access, permits and honest advice.
summary: Tholung Monastery is a Nyingma gompa at about 2,400 m in remote upper Dzongu, inside the buffer zone of Khangchendzonga National Park. It guards sealed boxes of relics and manuscripts, said to have been brought here for safety during the Gorkha invasions, which are shown to pilgrims only at the Kamsel ceremony every three years. Reaching it needs a Dzongu permit, a long drive and a walk.
intro: Tholung stands on a forested shelf high above the Rongyong valley, in the upper reaches of Dzongu where the road gives out and paths continue towards the Kangchenjunga massif. Wikipedia describes it as one of the most sacred monasteries in Sikkim. The site was revealed as a holy place by the fourth Lhatsun, Kunzang Jigmed Gyatso, in 1760, and a monastery was built here in 1789 by Pema Dechhen Gyatso. The present building is a later reconstruction.

Its fame rests on what it keeps. During the Gorkha invasions of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, manuscripts, masks, statues and other treasures from monasteries elsewhere in Sikkim were carried to this remote place for safety. They are still stored in more than a dozen sealed boxes under the supervision of the Government of Sikkim, together with a metal chorten said to hold the ashes of an incarnation of Lhatsun Chenpo, the lama who helped found the kingdom's Buddhist tradition.

Tholung is not a casual stop. You need a Dzongu permit, a reliable vehicle to the road-head in upper Dzongu, and the fitness for a walk of several hours on a steep forest trail; road and bridge damage since 2023 has changed access more than once. Most visitors come for the Kamsel, when pilgrims walk up from across Sikkim. At other times the monastery may be locked. Ask us about current access and check current status before you travel.

story.title: Treasures carried into the forest
story.text: In the late 18th century the Gorkha armies of Nepal pushed into western Sikkim, and the kingdom's capital moved east to Tumlong for safety in 1793, as Wikipedia's article on Tumlong records. Monasteries in the path of the fighting faced the loss of their most precious objects. According to the Wikipedia article on Tholung Monastery, manuscripts and relics from other gompas were brought to Tholung, deep in Dzongu and far from any invasion route, and placed there for protection. They never went back. Today they rest in more than a dozen sealed boxes, overseen by the state, and are opened only once every three years in the Kamsel ceremony, when the objects are taken out, aired in the sun and shown to pilgrims before being sealed again. The festival notes in our own Tholung Kamsel page describe the ceremony as overseen by Sikkim's Ecclesiastical Affairs Department, and the 2021 Kamsel was held from 23 to 26 November rather than in spring. Among the treasures is a metal chorten said to hold the ashes of an incarnation of Lhatsun Chenpo.
story.source: Wikipedia, Tholung Monastery and Tumlong; Ecclesiastical Affairs Department, Government of Sikkim

little_known.fact: Tholung follows the Nyingma school, and its site was revealed as sacred by the fourth Lhatsun, Kunzang Jigmed Gyatso, in 1760, nearly thirty years before the first monastery was built.
The monastery lies in the buffer zone of Khangchendzonga National Park, which UNESCO inscribed in 2016 as India's first mixed natural and cultural World Heritage Site.
little_known.source: Wikipedia, Tholung Monastery and Khangchendzonga National Park

little_known.fact: The Kamsel was traditionally held in spring, but dates vary: the 2021 ceremony took place in late November, so always confirm the year's dates.
little_known.source: Ecclesiastical Affairs Department, Sikkim; news reports 2021

highlights.title: The Kamsel relic display
highlights.text: Every three years the sealed boxes are opened and their contents aired and shown to pilgrims over a few days. It is the one time most people see inside Tholung's treasury. Dates are fixed by the religious authorities and announced in advance; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: The walk through forest
highlights.text: From the road-head in upper Dzongu a trail climbs through mixed forest of oak, magnolia and rhododendron, crossing streams on wooden bridges. The walk takes several hours each way, depending on where vehicles can reach after the latest monsoon. Go with a local guide.

highlights.title: A monastery that kept Sikkim's past
highlights.text: Tholung's treasures came from other gompas during the Gorkha invasions and were never returned. Standing here, you are at one of the places where Sikkim's Buddhist heritage was quite literally carried to safety. Few visitors make the effort.

highlights.title: Upper Dzongu villages
highlights.text: The approach passes through the upper villages of Dzongu, with cardamom, paddy terraces and Lepcha houses. Spending a night or two in a homestay nearby breaks the journey and gives you time to walk without hurry.

highlights.title: Edge of Khangchendzonga National Park
highlights.text: Tholung lies in the buffer zone of the national park. Birdlife in the forest is rich, and on clear days the slopes above hint at the snow peaks beyond. Stay on trails and carry all rubbish out.

how_to_reach.text: Drive from Gangtok via Mangan into Upper Dzongu, about 4–5 hours to the furthest point vehicles can reach, which has shifted with road and bridge repairs. Your Dzongu permit must be arranged first. A local 4x4 from Mangan or your homestay is often best for the last stretch.

From the road-head the walk to Tholung takes several hours each way on a steep forest trail. Most people sleep in an upper Dzongu homestay the night before, walk up early and return the same day, or stay at simple pilgrim accommodation during the Kamsel when it is offered.

Plan a night in Gangtok, then a night in a Dzongu homestay before the walk. From NJP or Bagdogra the drive to Gangtok takes 4.5–5 hours on NH10, longer via Kalimpong or Algarah when NH10 is closed by slides.

where_to_stay: There is no hotel near Tholung. Stay in a Lepcha homestay in upper Dzongu, such as Mayal Lyang at Passingdang or another family we know closer to the road-head, for about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals. During the Kamsel, pilgrims sometimes use simple community or monastery shelter; ask us what is available in the year you go. Mangan, across the Teesta, has the nearest hotels, including Hotel Tamarind, but it adds a long drive to an already long day.
tips: Confirm current road and bridge conditions in upper Dzongu before you plan the walk.
Start walking early, carry water, snacks and a rain jacket, and wear proper trekking shoes.
Dress modestly, remove shoes inside and ask before photographing any relic or interior.
In Kamsel years, book your homestay well ahead, as pilgrims fill upper Dzongu.
Carry cash from Mangan; there are no ATMs in Dzongu.

experiences.title: Walking the pilgrim trail to Tholung
experiences.summary: Climb from the road-head in upper Dzongu through mixed forest to Tholung Monastery and back in a long, steady day. A real walk, not a stroll, rewarded with quiet forest, streams and one of Sikkim's most sacred monasteries.
body: The trail to Tholung starts where vehicles stop in upper Dzongu. That point has moved over the years as roads have been extended and then damaged by slides, so your guide will confirm it the evening before. From there the path climbs steadily through forest, with stone steps, roots and stream crossings on simple bridges. Expect several hours up and a little less down.

The forest is the reward on the way: tall oaks and magnolias, rhododendron and bamboo, moss on every branch, and birdsong in the mornings. It is humid even in autumn, and the last section to the monastery is steep. Take it slowly, drink water and eat on the way. At about 2,400 m the altitude is moderate, but the climbing makes it feel harder.

Walk with a local guide from Dzongu, which is both safer and the respectful way to approach a sacred site. Start at first light so you are back before dark. Outside the Kamsel the monastery may be locked; your guide can check whether a caretaker will be present.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Tholung Monastery?
faqs.a: It depends on where vehicles can reach in upper Dzongu at the time, which changes after monsoon damage. Most walkers should plan several hours up and a little less down, as a full day. Your guide will confirm the start point and timing. Ask us about current access before you go.

faqs.q: Is the Tholung trek difficult?
faqs.a: It is moderate to strenuous. The trail climbs steadily through forest with steep sections, steps and stream crossings, and it is often wet. Altitude is modest at about 2,400 m, but you need reasonable fitness and good shoes. It is not suitable for people with knee or heart problems.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for Tholung?
faqs.a: Yes, we strongly recommend a local guide. The trail is not signposted, conditions change after monsoons, and Tholung is a sacred site where local guidance helps. A guide costs about ₹1,000–2,000 for the day, arranged through your homestay. Never walk alone in upper Dzongu.

experiences.title: Joining pilgrims at the Tholung Kamsel
experiences.best_time: Kamsel years only; dates announced in advance
experiences.cost: Free entry; travel and stay ≈ ₹6,000–10,000 per person
experiences.summary: Once every three years Tholung's sealed relics are opened, aired and shown to the faithful. Walk up with pilgrims from across Sikkim and see the monastery at its fullest. Respectful visitors are welcome; plan early and confirm dates.
body: The Kamsel, also spelled Kamsil or Khamsel, is the ceremony at which Tholung's boxes of relics and manuscripts are unsealed, brought out into the sun and shown to pilgrims over a few days, then sealed again. It is overseen by Sikkim's Ecclesiastical Affairs Department, and monks lead prayers throughout. For many Sikkimese Buddhists it is a pilgrimage of a lifetime.

Dates are set by the religious authorities and announced ahead of time. The ceremony was traditionally held in spring, but the 2021 Kamsel took place in late November, so do not assume a month. In a Kamsel year, upper Dzongu fills with pilgrims, vehicles queue at the road-head, and homestays book out early.

Visitors should treat it as a religious event first. Dress modestly, walk clockwise, follow the queue and the monks' instructions, and ask before taking any photograph; photography of the relics may not be allowed. We plan Kamsel trips with an extra night so that a delay on the road does not cost you the day.

faqs.q: When is the next Tholung Kamsel?
faqs.a: The Kamsel is held once every three years, and dates are announced by the religious authorities. The 2021 ceremony ran from 23 to 26 November, but the cycle and month can shift, so we do not guess future dates. Ask us for the confirmed dates and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend the Tholung Kamsel?
faqs.a: Respectful visitors are generally welcome alongside pilgrims, provided they hold a Dzongu permit. Dress modestly, follow the monks' instructions and the queue, and ask before photographing anything. Expect crowds and simple facilities, and book your homestay early.

faqs.q: What is shown at the Kamsel?
faqs.a: The sealed boxes of Tholung's treasures, which include manuscripts, statues and other relics that, according to Wikipedia, were brought from other monasteries for protection during the Gorkha invasions. They are aired in the sun, shown to pilgrims and then sealed again for another three years.

experiences.title: A night in upper Dzongu before Tholung
experiences.summary: Sleep in a Lepcha homestay in upper Dzongu the night before the Tholung walk. You start fresh at first light, eat a proper dinner, and hear your hosts' own stories of the monastery and the Kamsel.
body: Tholung is too far for a day trip from Gangtok and a stretch even from Mangan. A night in upper Dzongu solves that. Families in the upper villages host guests in simple rooms with home-cooked meals, and many have walked to Tholung themselves for the Kamsel. Ask them what it means to them; it is a better introduction than any guidebook.

Dinner is usually rice, dal, vegetables and greens from the fields, sometimes with local chicken or pork, and breakfast can be packed for an early start. Your host can arrange a guide and, if needed, a local vehicle to the road-head. Pay directly and fairly; homestay income matters in upper Dzongu.
Bring a torch, a warm layer for the evening and cash. Mobile signal is weak or absent in many upper villages. Your Dzongu permit must cover the dates of your stay.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for Tholung Monastery?
faqs.a: Stay in a Lepcha homestay in upper Dzongu, as close to the road-head as roads allow. There are no hotels in the reserve. Rates are about ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals. Your host can arrange a guide and vehicle. In Kamsel years, book well in advance.

faqs.q: Can I do Tholung as a day trip from Gangtok?
faqs.a: No, not realistically. The drive to upper Dzongu takes 4–5 hours and the walk several more each way. Plan at least two nights in Dzongu, with the walk on the middle day. A Mangan base is possible but adds driving to a long day.

faqs.q: Is there mobile signal in upper Dzongu?
faqs.a: Coverage is weak or absent in many upper villages and on the Tholung trail. Some homestays have a spot with a signal. Tell family you may be out of contact for a day or two, carry a printed copy of your permit, and agree a pickup time with your driver in advance.

experiences.title: Visiting Tholung with respect
experiences.best_time: When a caretaker or monks are present
experiences.summary: Tholung is one of Sikkim's most sacred monasteries, and its treasures belong to the whole Buddhist community. Learn what to expect when you arrive, how to behave, and why the doors may be closed outside the Kamsel.
body: Tholung follows the Nyingma school, the oldest tradition of Tibetan Buddhism and the one closely linked with Guru Padmasambhava in Sikkim. Outside the Kamsel the treasury is sealed, and the monastery may be locked, with a caretaker living nearby. If it is open, a monk or caretaker may show you the prayer hall.

Remove your shoes and hat before entering, walk clockwise around the building and any chortens, keep your voice low and do not touch altars, statues or offerings. Ask before taking any photograph, and accept a no. A small offering placed where your guide shows you is appreciated but not required.
Remember why the relics are here: they were carried into this remote forest to keep them safe in a time of war. Treat the place as you would a shrine at home. Take all rubbish back down the trail.

faqs.q: Is Tholung Monastery open every day?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Outside the Kamsel, the monastery may be locked, and opening depends on whether a caretaker or monks are present. Your Dzongu host or guide can try to check in advance. Even if the doors are closed, the walk and the setting are worth the effort for keen walkers.

faqs.q: Can I photograph the relics at Tholung?
faqs.a: Photography of the relics and the interior may not be allowed, especially during the Kamsel. Always ask the monks or caretaker, and accept a no. Photographs of the building's exterior and the forest are usually fine, but avoid photographing pilgrims without permission.

faqs.q: Which school of Buddhism is Tholung?
faqs.a: Tholung follows the Nyingma school, the oldest of the Tibetan Buddhist traditions, according to Wikipedia. Many of Sikkim's older monasteries belong to it, including Pemayangtse and Tashiding. The site's link with the Lhatsun lineage connects it to the founding of Sikkim's Buddhist tradition.

faqs.q: Where is Tholung Monastery?
faqs.a: Tholung Monastery is in remote upper Dzongu, Mangan district (North Sikkim), at about 2,400 m in the buffer zone of Khangchendzonga National Park. It lies above the Rongyong valley, reached by a long drive from Mangan into upper Dzongu and then a walk of several hours on a forest trail.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Tholung Monastery?
faqs.a: Yes. Tholung lies inside Dzongu, so you need a Dzongu permit issued in Mangan, usually arranged by your homestay. Because the monastery is in the national park's buffer zone, ask us whether any extra formality applies in the year you go. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Tholung Kamsel?
faqs.a: The Kamsel, also spelled Kamsil, is the ceremony held once every three years when Tholung's sealed relics are opened, aired in the sun and shown to pilgrims. It is overseen by Sikkim's Ecclesiastical Affairs Department and draws pilgrims from across the state. Dates are announced in advance.

faqs.q: Why are relics kept at Tholung?
faqs.a: According to Wikipedia, manuscripts and relics from other Sikkimese monasteries were brought to remote Tholung for protection during the Gorkha invasions of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. They remain there in sealed boxes supervised by the Government of Sikkim, together with a metal chorten said to hold an incarnation's ashes.

faqs.q: How old is Tholung Monastery?
faqs.a: Wikipedia records that the site was revealed as sacred by the fourth Lhatsun, Kunzang Jigmed Gyatso, in 1760, and that Pema Dechhen Gyatso built a monastery here in 1789. The present building is a later reconstruction. The relics it guards are older still.

faqs.q: How fit do I need to be for Tholung?
faqs.a: Reasonably fit. The walk takes several hours each way on a steep, often wet forest trail, at moderate altitude of about 2,400 m. If you can walk 5–6 hours on hill paths with breaks, you can manage. People with knee, heart or breathing problems should not attempt it.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Tholung?
faqs.a: October and November bring dry trails and clear skies, and March and April are pleasant with flowering trees. December to February can be cold and icy higher up, and June to September brings heavy rain, leeches and road damage. In a Kamsel year, plan around the announced dates.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Tholung Monastery?
faqs.a: Tholung lies in Dzongu, where rules for foreign nationals have varied over the years. Foreigners first need the online Sikkim restricted area permit and then specific clearance for Dzongu. Please ask us before planning so we can check the current position. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Tholung?
faqs.a: Plan at least two nights in Dzongu, with the walk on the middle day, plus travel from Gangtok. In a Kamsel year or after monsoon damage, add a buffer night. A three-night Dzongu stay lets you combine Tholung with village walks and time with your hosts.
